By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press
It was cool and gray on the first day of October in downtown Detroit.

Years ago, the locals recognized it as postseason baseball weather. But now, relegated to watching 10 other teams try for a World Series championship, Detroit Tigers fans see it only as the start of a cold winter ahead.
Miguel Cabrera knows all about the postseason: He’s made five trips, beginning with his breakout rookie season as a 20-year-old with the Marlins in 2003.

But while his team is not going to the postseason – the Tigers wrapped up a 64-98 season a day earlier – he delivered the best news about his rehabilitation from a ruptured right biceps by referencing it.
Right now, he said, speaking at his foundation’s “Miggy Ball 24” event, he can do everything with his right arm. Maybe even swing a baseball bat.

“If we were going to play in the playoffs, I think I’d be able to be ready right now,” Cabrera said. “But they don’t want to push me, because we got a lot of time. But I talked to the trainers, the doctor and if we got a chance to go to the playoffs – if it was a big chance – I could play right now.”
Cabrera was lost for the season, blowing out his bicep muscle during a swing on June 12. He has spent nearly all of the final four months of the season rehabbing near his home in Miami and expects to make a full recovery in time for spring training.

“It was really tough, because it was kind of sad to watch the games on TV,” he said. “But at the same time, I had a lot of time to think about, to see what I want to do the next five years in Detroit. I hope I can be mentally strong and physically to come in here and play good baseball.”
The mental part has never been a problem for Cabrera. Physically, though, he has been hampered by injuries in each of the last three seasons. He will play next season at age 36.
The glass half-full outlook? His body will respond to the lengthy rest it’s received since June.

“You gotta think positive,” he said. “I think that way. I think things happen for a reason. I don’t want to be hurt, but I gotta think about everything I didn’t do this year and I’m trying to focus about next year.”
Cabrera’s injury is rare in baseball, but he doesn’t chalk it up to just bad luck: He’s been beating himself up for years by playing injured.

“I played a lot of years hurt and not taken care of my body when I was hurt,” he said. “So I think I paid the price the last three years. So right now, I’m focused to not be hurt and strong and I’m trying to go out there and give everything everyday.”

The glass half-empty outlook? He is only getting older, more prone to injuries, and despite his elite hitting aptitude, his sharpness could decline after nearly a season off. Oh, yes, and he is owed $154 million for the next five seasons.
“I think I got something to show next year,” he said. “Something to give back to the team and the fans and I feel more motivated right now about that.”

Cabrera has fallen from the surest of things in the middle of the Tigers’ batting order and at first base to a relative unknown because of the injury. He expects to start swinging a bat again in December.

Defensively, he still grades out as a good first baseman, but the Tigers will likely try to play him at designated hitter much more often than they have in the past, in the name of trying to keep him healthy.

“I always focus on how I can help the team be better,” he said. “So (general manager) Al (Avila), (manager Ron Gardenhire) will sit with me and talk about that. I’m very open to talk, but I like to play first.
“But if they decide to give me a lot more days at DH, I gotta think about it, if it’s better for the team and better for my health, I gotta say, ‘Yeah.’”

At full health, the most likely scenario is that Cabrera remains the Tigers’ full-time first baseman, with more starts at DH, but not nearly as many as some might expect: His injury impacted the team greatly on defense this season.
Cabrera admitted that he gets the itch to pick up a bat – “I miss it a lot,” he said – and while he worked with young kids during the event at The Corner ballpark, he certainly felt that itch.

The event, an initiative of the Miguel Cabrera Foundation, is in its fourth year. It began in Venezuela before moving to Florida because of the turmoil in his homeland. On Monday, kids participated in a recreational competition and received instruction, autographs and pictures with Cabrera.

It was the foundation’s first event held in Detroit.
“I think teaching the kids the right way to play baseball, teaching them how to compete the right way, that’s why I do this,” he said. “I do this to do something they can learn about the game.
“I don’t have a chance to have this in my country back in Venezuela, so that’s very nice that we can do it here in Detroit.”
But he is already thinking about returning to Comerica Park next spring.

“Yeah,” he said, when asked if what he’s seen out of this year’s team excites him for the future. “That’s a good thing. They never give up, they always go out there and try to play 100 percent. If they win or lose, they play the same way, so you see that. I feel proud the way they played.”
